slides.text: In 1922, an audience in New York sat in a theater and watched a concert played on light.
The instrument was the Clavilux, built in 1919 by Thomas Wilfred, a Danish-born artist working in New York.
The name means “light played by key.” Wilfred sat at a console and shaped moving color on a screen.
He called the art lumia, and meant it as a new art of its own, with light as the only material.
From the late 1920s he built smaller Clavilux models for the home. He hoped they would become as common as the radio.
In 1963, the Museum of Modern Art commissioned one for its reopened galleries: Lumia Suite, Opus 158.
It played in its own dark room at the museum from 1964 until 1980, long after Wilfred died in 1968.
Then it was taken apart and packed into storage.
In 2017, Yale restored it with hand-blown replacement bulbs and Wilfred's own technical manual, and it was shown again.
